refuted.title: Hook path containment check removed: traversal in `hooks remove`/`hooks edit`
refuted.description:
`hookFileName` comes straight from the positional CLI argument (`hookFileName := args[0]`, line 146) and is concatenated into `hookFile` without any cleaning or containment check. This change deletes the guard that previously stood between that concatenation and the sink:

    hookFileAbs, err := filepath.Abs(hookFile)
    if !strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, hooksDir) { return fmt.Errorf("hook file %s is outside of hookDir %s", ...) }

With the guard gone, a value such as `../../../../etc/cron.d/foo` escapes the hooks directory and `os.Remove` acts on an arbitrary path. The identical guard was removed from `editHooksCmd` (same root cause), where the escaped path is handed to the editor process and then to `os.Chmod(hookFile, 0700)` at line 236, allowing an arbitrary file outside the hooks directory to be opened for editing and made mode 0700.

Scope note, stated plainly: the traversal string is supplied by whoever invokes the CLI, so on a normal invocation the user is only acting on their own authority and the removal is a hardening regression rather than a boundary crossing. It becomes a real privilege boundary crossing where `uniget` is granted elevated rights to a lower-privileged principal — e.g. a `sudoers` entry that permits only `/usr/local/bin/uniget`, or any wrapper/automation that passes an externally supplied hook name — because the process then writes to root-owned paths chosen by the caller. I could not confirm such an invocation from this repository, hence the low confidence.
refuted.exploit_scenario: A host grants a low-privileged operator a restricted sudo rule for the package tool only (`operator ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/uniget`). The operator runs `sudo uniget hooks remove --type pre-install '../../../../etc/sudoers.d/00-hardening'`. Because the containment check is gone, `hookFile` resolves outside `<prefix>/etc/uniget/hooks/pre-install`, `fileExists` succeeds, and `os.Remove` deletes the root-owned file. The same path via `sudo uniget hooks edit --type pre-install '../../../../etc/cron.d/job'` opens an arbitrary root-owned file in the editor and then chmods it 0700.
refuted.recommendation: Restore containment before the sink in both `removeHooksCmd` and `editHooksCmd`, and prefer rejecting the name outright over cleaning it: verify `hookFileName` contains no `/` and is not `.`/`..` (e.g. `if hookFileName != filepath.Base(hookFileName) { return error }`), then additionally check `filepath.Clean`/`filepath.Abs` of the joined path is prefixed by the absolute hooks directory (comparing against `hooksDirAbs + string(os.PathSeparator)` so sibling directories like `/etc/uniget-evil` do not pass the prefix test).

verification.reason: 3/3 verifier(s) agreed — The diff does really delete the `filepath.Abs`/`strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, hooksDir)` containment check from both `removeHooksCmd` and `editHooksCmd` (cmd/uniget/hooks.go, removed lines around 160 and 226), so the code-level regression is genuine — but there is no privilege boundary for it to cross. The only source of `hookFileName` is `args[0]` of a local CLI command (line 146 / line 203); the sole entry point is the cobra command registered in `initHooksCmd` (lines 39/46), i.e. the person invoking the binary, who by definition already holds the process's file permissions. The claimed escalation via a restricted `sudoers` rule does not hold either, because the same CLI already offers `uniget hooks add --source <any path>` (lines 88-135: copies an arbitrary file into the hooks dir and `os.Chmod` 0700) plus `uniget hooks run` (lines 305-325, executing every file in that dir via `runHook`), so anyone permitted to run uniget as root already has arbitrary root code execution regardless of this check — the containment guard never protected a boundary. Refuted on source/impact, not on absence of a caller. Searched: I looked for (a) any remaining containment/sanitisation of the hook name: searched cmd/uniget for `filepath.Abs`, `Clean`, `HasPrefix` around hooks — none remain in hooks.go after this change, and `testHookCmd` (line 340-350) never had one, so the pattern predates the diff; (b) any non-CLI caller that could feed untrusted data into removeHooksCmd/editHooksCmd — searched the repo for `removeHooksCmd`/`editHooksCmd`/`hooks remove|edit` and found only the cobra registrations in `initHooksCmd`, no server, daemon, or manifest-driven invocation; (c) any privilege-boundary deployment (sudoers/setuid wrapper) — searched the whole repo for `sudo`, no matches, and packaging/docs contain no restricted-sudo rule. I also verified `hooksDir` is always absolute (cmd/uniget/main.go 93-145), so the removed prefix check had been functional; the removal is a hardening regression, but the same binary grants the invoking principal arbitrary file placement and execution through `hooks add`/`hooks run`, so no attacker gains anything they did not already have.

The claimed escalation via a restricted `sudoers` rule does not hold either, because the same CLI already offers `uniget hooks add --source <any path>` (lines 88-135: copies an arbitrary file into the hooks dir and `os.Chmod` 0700) plus `uniget hooks run` (lines 305-325, executing every file in that dir via `runHook`), so anyone permitted to run uniget as root already has arbitrary root code execution regardless of this check — the containment guard never protected a boundary. Refuted on source/impact, not on absence of a caller.

The diff does remove the `filepath.Abs` + `strings.HasPrefix(hookFileAbs, hooksDir)` containment check (and the Lstat symlink checks) from `removeHooksCmd`/`editHooksCmd`/`processHooks`, so the code facts are as described. But working backwards from the sink, `os.Remove(hookFile)` at cmd/uniget/hooks.go:171 is reachable only through the cobra `hooks remove` RunE, whose `args[0]` (line 146) can only be supplied on the command line of a locally invoked binary; the only program entry is `rootCmd.Execute()` at cmd/uniget/main.go:486, and no daemon, RPC, `SetArgs`, or metadata-driven caller exists (searched for `removeHooksCmd|editHooksCmd|SetArgs|rootCmd.Execute`, 9 hits, all registration/definition). The path therefore stays inside a single privilege domain — the operator passing the traversal string already has the process's authority — and the claimed boundary crossing depends entirely on a hypothetical sudoers/wrapper deployment that does not exist in this repository (`sudo` has zero matches anywhere in the tree, no setuid, no service unit). This is a genuine hardening/defence-in-depth regression worth a human's attention, but not an exploitable path traversal as described.

The removal of the `filepath.Abs`/`HasPrefix` containment check at cmd/uniget/hooks.go:167 and 219 is real (visible in the diff), but the only source for `hookFileName` is `args[0]` of a locally invoked cobra command (`removeHooksCmd` line 132, `editHooksCmd` line 180); I searched for any other caller and found the commands are only registered in `initHooksCmd` (lines 41, 48) and nothing in pkg/ or elsewhere feeds hook names from a file, network, or metadata source, so the "attacker" is the operator running the process with their own privileges. The claimed privilege boundary rests entirely on an out-of-repo sudoers rule, and even in that hypothetical the same rule already yields root through code this MR does not touch: `hooks add --source /tmp/evil` copies an arbitrary file into the hooks dir and chmods it 0700 (lines 118-127), `hooks run` then executes it as root, and `hooks test <path>` builds `hookFile` from `args[0]` with no containment check at all (lines 330-350) and execs it. The deletion is therefore a hardening regression in defence-in-depth, not a crossing of any privilege boundary that the unchanged code does not already permit.
